title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
description: Splice two sorted lists into one sorted list using a dummy head and a tail pointer. Iterative, O(1) extra space beyond the dummy.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I'm given the heads of two singly linked lists, each already sorted in ascending order, and I need to return the head of a single merged list that's also sorted. The intent is to splice the existing nodes together rather than allocate new ones — so I'll be rewriting `next` pointers in place."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Either list empty — return the other one as-is?
• Both empty — return null?
• Mutation OK — can I rewire the existing nodes' `next`, or do I need fresh nodes?
• Duplicate values across the two lists — both should appear in the output (stable)?
• Sort order — confirming ascending? (If descending, the comparator flips.)
sections.why: The mutation question matters for space — splicing existing nodes is O(1) extra; allocating new nodes is O(n+m). The duplicate-handling question signals you've thought about stability: if [1,2,4] and [1,3,4] both contain 1 and 4, the output is [1,1,2,3,4,4] not [1,2,3,4]. And asking 'are both empty' surfaces the cleanest invariant — your loop should produce null naturally without an upfront `if`.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious copy-and-sort solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is: walk both lists, push every value into an array, sort it, then build a fresh linked list from the sorted array. That's O((n+m) log (n+m)) time and O(n+m) extra space. Functionally correct, but it throws away the precondition — the two lists are ALREADY sorted, so we shouldn't need a sort. The right structure is a merge step from mergesort: walk both heads in parallel, splice whichever is smaller, advance that pointer. O(n+m) time, O(1) extra space if we splice in place."
sections.why: Two reasons to name copy-and-sort out loud. (1) It proves you can see the obvious answer before reaching for the merge — important because the merge isn't obvious if you've never seen mergesort. (2) Stating 'we shouldn't need to sort because the inputs are already sorted' frames the merge as exploiting the precondition, which is exactly the right intuition for why merge runs in linear time instead of n log n.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to the dummy-head splice pattern?
sections.say:
"This is the canonical dummy-head pattern. Whenever I'm building a linked list incrementally — appending nodes one at a time — I want a dummy sentinel at the front so the first append works the same as every subsequent append. Without a dummy, the first node is special: I'd have to write 'if head is null, head = newNode; else tail.next = newNode' on every iteration. With a dummy, I always do `tail.next = newNode; tail = tail.next`, and return `dummy.next` at the end. The sentinel exists only to absorb that first-append asymmetry.

The loop itself is a two-pointer walk on the inputs (a and b) and a one-pointer build on the output (tail). I compare `a.val <= b.val` — using `<=` rather than `<` for stability so equal values from `a` go in first — splice the winner, advance that input pointer, advance tail. When one list runs out, the other is already sorted, so I just attach the survivor with `tail.next = a || b` and we're done."
sections.why: Naming the dummy-head pattern *and* what it buys you ('first append is no longer a special case') is the move. 'Use a dummy' alone is a recipe; explaining why — to eliminate the head/tail asymmetry — shows you understand when to reach for the pattern in OTHER problems where you're building a linked list incrementally (Add Two Numbers, Reverse Between m and n, basically every linked-list constructor). The stability argument with `<=` is the small detail that separates careful candidates from sloppy ones.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure the model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a balanced merge with a duplicate, an empty-list edge, and an asymmetric merge where one list ends much earlier than the other.

examples.note: Classic merge with duplicates — the `<=` comparator keeps a's 1 before b's 1 (stable).
examples.trace:
init: dummy→null, tail=dummy
iter1: 1 <= 1 → splice a(1), a=[2,4]. tail=1.   merged=[1]
iter2: 2 > 1 → splice b(1), b=[3,4]. tail=1.    merged=[1,1]
iter3: 2 <= 3 → splice a(2), a=[4]. tail=2.    merged=[1,1,2]
iter4: 4 > 3 → splice b(3), b=[4]. tail=3.     merged=[1,1,2,3]
iter5: 4 <= 4 → splice a(4), a=null. tail=4.   merged=[1,1,2,3,4]
loop exits (a is null). Attach b=[4] → merged=[1,1,2,3,4,4]
return dummy.next = node(1)

examples.note: Empty list — loop never executes; `tail.next = a || b` attaches b directly.
examples.trace:
init: dummy→null, tail=dummy
loop check: a is null → never enter
Attach: tail.next = a || b = b = [0]. merged=[0]
return dummy.next = node(0)

examples.note: Asymmetric — b empties first, then the rest of a (just node 5) attaches in one move.
examples.trace:
init: dummy→null, tail=dummy
iter1: 1 <= 2 → splice a(1), a=[5]. tail=1.   merged=[1]
iter2: 5 > 2 → splice b(2), b=[3,4]. tail=2.  merged=[1,2]
iter3: 5 > 3 → splice b(3), b=[4]. tail=3.    merged=[1,2,3]
iter4: 5 > 4 → splice b(4), b=null. tail=4.   merged=[1,2,3,4]
loop exits (b is null). Attach a=[5] → merged=[1,2,3,4,5]
return dummy.next = node(1)

sections.why: Tracing surfaces the two bugs this problem rewards. (1) The `<=` vs `<` choice is invisible until you trace two equal values — `<=` keeps a's value first (stable); `<` would still merge correctly but with reversed order at ties, which fails the stability requirement that some interview variants care about. (2) The empty-list and asymmetric traces both confirm that `tail.next = a || b` is the one-liner that handles 'one list still has nodes' for free — no extra loop needed because the survivor is already a fully-formed sorted list.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Both lists empty (a=null, b=null) → loop never runs, `tail.next = null || null = null`, return dummy.next = null. ✓
• One list empty → loop never runs, the survivor attaches in one move. ✓
• All values in a smaller than all in b (e.g. a=[1,2,3], b=[4,5,6]) → loop drains a completely, then b attaches as-is.
• Identical lists (a=b in values) → the `<=` comparator interleaves them: a₁, b₁, a₂, b₂, …
• Lists with a single node each → one iteration of the loop, then one survivor attach. Tests the dummy-head plumbing.
• Very long lists (millions of nodes) → O(n+m) time, O(1) space; no risk of recursion stack overflow because this is iterative."
sections.why: Walking the both-empty and one-empty cases shows the algorithm degrades gracefully — no `if (!a || !b)` short-circuit needed. The 'all values in a smaller' case is worth naming because it exercises the survivor-attach path heavily; if you had a bug where you forgot to attach the leftover, that case would silently truncate. The iterative-vs-recursive call-out also flags that you've thought about real-world stack limits, which matters for production code.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n + m) — each node from either list is examined and spliced exactly once. The body of the loop does a fixed amount of pointer work, so no amortization argument is needed.

Space is O(1) — one dummy node, one tail pointer, no auxiliary structures. We're rewiring the existing nodes, not allocating new ones.

If you wanted to extend to 'merge k sorted lists', the natural approach is to apply this exact `mergeTwo` k-1 times pairwise — but that's O(n*k). The better approach is divide-and-conquer pairwise (merge in pairs, then pairs of pairs) which gets to O(n log k), or a min-heap of size k for the same bound. Same merge-two primitive underneath, just better orchestration."
sections.why: The 'each node spliced exactly once' argument is the clean defense against an interviewer who asks 'why O(n+m) and not something else?'. The merge-k extension is the natural follow-up (LeetCode 23) and proves you see merge-two as a reusable primitive rather than this one problem's solution — that's how it shows up in MergeSort, Merge k Sorted Lists, and any external-merge variant where data doesn't fit in memory.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the iterative merge with a dummy head. Input is { a, b } as two pre-sorted arrays. Watch the tail pointer splice the smaller head each iteration; after the loop, the leftover survivor attaches in one move.
trace: const { a: arrA, b: arrB } = input;
const toList = (arr) => { const d = { val: 0, next: null }; let c = d; for (const v of arr) { c.next = { val: v, next: null }; c = c.next; } return d.next; };
const toArr = (n) => { const out = []; while (n) { out.push(n.val); n = n.next; } return out; };
yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — a=${JSON.stringify(arrA)}, b=${JSON.stringify(arrB)}`, state: { a: toArr(a), b: toArr(b) } };
yield { line: 2, label: 'create dummy sentinel', state: { a: toArr(a), b: toArr(b), dummy: 'sentinel' } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'tail = dummy', state: { a: toArr(a), b: toArr(b), tail: 'dummy', merged: toArr(dummy.next) } };
yield { line: 4, label: `loop iter ${iter} — compare a.val=${a.val} vs b.val=${b.val}`, state: { a: toArr(a), b: toArr(b), tailVal: tail.val, merged: toArr(dummy.next) } };
yield { line: 5, label: `a.val (${a.val}) <= b.val (${b.val}) — splice a, advance a`, state: { a: toArr(a.next), b: toArr(b), merged: toArr(dummy.next) } };
yield { line: 6, label: `a.val (${a.val}) > b.val (${b.val}) — splice b, advance b`, state: { a: toArr(a), b: toArr(b.next), merged: toArr(dummy.next) } };
yield { line: 7, label: `advance tail → ${tail.val}`, state: { a: toArr(a), b: toArr(b), tailVal: tail.val, merged: toArr(dummy.next) } };
yield { line: 9, label: `attach leftover survivor: ${a ? 'a=' + JSON.stringify(toArr(a)) : (b ? 'b=' + JSON.stringify(toArr(b)) : 'none')}`, state: { merged: toArr(dummy.next) } };
yield { line: 10, label: `return dummy.next`, state: { merged: toArr(dummy.next), returns: JSON.stringify(toArr(dummy.next)) } };

reference.approach: Dummy head + tail pointer, splice the smaller head (merge step)
notes: A dummy head removes the special case 'which list becomes the new head?'.
Don't forget to attach the remaining tail — one list will still have nodes.
Use <= (not <) for stability across equal values.
reference.crux: Dummy head + tail pointer: splice whichever head is smaller and advance it; when one list empties, attach the survivor whole with `tail.next = a || b` — already sorted.
cruxDistractors: Collect both lists' values into an array, sort it, and rebuild a list — ignores the sorted precondition, O((n+m) log(n+m)).
Recurse: return whichever head is smaller with its .next merged against the other list — correct, but O(n+m) call-stack space.
After the loop, walk the leftover survivor and append each node one at a time to the tail.

alternates.label: Recursive (divide at the smaller head)
alternates.when: Reach for this when the interviewer wants the recursive formulation, or when the merge is a sub-call in a recursive algorithm (e.g. merge sort) and the call-stack depth is bounded. In JS the recursion depth is n+m, so for large lists prefer the iterative version.
notes: Each call either consumes one node from `a` or one from `b`, so there are at most n+m frames on the call stack.
No dummy head needed — the return value of each recursive call wires the next pointer naturally.
O(n+m) stack space; for long lists this risks a stack overflow, which is why the iterative version is generally preferred in production.

questions.q: Why use a dummy head node?
options: Lets the merge run in O(1) space by reusing the dummy as the output head pointer
Removes the special case of picking the new head
Anchors the merge so cyclic inputs cannot loop the tail back to the start
Forces both lists to start at the same address so `<=` comparisons are stable
questions.explain: Without the sentinel each iteration would first have to ask "is this the first node?"; with it, `tail.next = node; tail = tail.next` is uniform and the real head is just `dummy.next`.

questions.q: After the while loop, why do we set tail.next = a || b?
options: To null-terminate the merged list — without it, tail.next still points at the last spliced node
One list may still have remaining sorted nodes to attach
To swap the two lists and rerun the merge in reverse order
It guards against a being null — `a || b` falls back to b when a was empty from the start
questions.explain: `while (a && b)` exits the instant one side is null, leaving the other's nodes unspliced; the survivor is already sorted and null-terminated, so one assignment attaches all of them.

questions.q: Time complexity for lists of length n and m?
options: O(n * m)
O((n + m) log (n + m))
O(n + m)
O(max(n, m)^2)
questions.explain: Each node is compared and spliced exactly once. The inputs arrive sorted, so there is no sort step and none of the log factor that copy-and-sort would cost.

options: dummy
dummy.next
tail
a
questions.explain: dummy is the sentinel; the real merged head is dummy.next.

questions.q: Concretely, what asymmetry does the dummy head eliminate?
options: Whether to compare with < or <=
The first append being special: without a dummy you'd need 'if head is null set head, else tail.next = node' every iteration
The need to track list lengths
Recursion versus iteration
questions.explain: With a dummy, every append is the uniform `tail.next = node; tail = tail.next` — the dummy absorbs the empty-head special case.

questions.q: Why does `tail.next = a || b` correctly finish the merge in one move?
options: It frees the unused list
The loop exits when one list is empty, and the other is already a fully sorted, terminated list
It reverses the leftover list first
It only works when both lists are empty
questions.explain: The survivor is itself sorted and null-terminated, so attaching its head splices all remaining nodes at once — no extra loop needed.

questions.q: Why does using `<=` (instead of `<`) preserve stability when values tie?
options: It avoids an infinite loop
On equal values it splices a's node first, keeping a's tied elements ahead of b's
<= is required for correct sorting
It makes the merge O(1) space
questions.explain: With `<=`, a tie sends a's node in first; `<` would still sort correctly but flip the order of equal elements, breaking stability.

questions.q: Why is this merge O(n + m) rather than O((n + m) log(n + m)) like copy-and-sort?
options: It uses a faster sort internally
The inputs are already sorted, so each node is examined and spliced exactly once with no sort step
Linked lists are inherently faster
The dummy head caches comparisons
questions.explain: The merge exploits the sorted precondition: a single linear pass splices every node once, avoiding the log factor a general sort needs.

questions.q: The canonical solution splices existing nodes in place. What does that buy over building a brand-new list?
options: It is stable while a new list is not
O(1) extra space — it rewires existing next pointers instead of allocating n + m new nodes
It runs in O(log n) time
It avoids the dummy head
questions.explain: In-place splicing reuses the input nodes, so extra space is just the dummy and tail pointer; allocating new nodes would be O(n + m) space.
